stem: Correlation refers to:
options: the statistical relationship/association between two variables (how they move/change together)
solution: Correlation refers to the statistical relationship or association between two variables — that is, the extent to which two variables are related, and how they tend to change/move together. For example, correlation studies whether (and how strongly) two things like income and consumption, or price and demand, or rainfall and crop yield, are related. If two variables tend to change together in a systematic way, they are said to be correlated. Correlation analysis measures the degree (strength) and the direction of this relationship between the two variables. Understanding what correlation means is a key prelims-relevant point. Correlation is the statistical relationship/association between two variables — how they change together.

stem: When two variables move in the SAME direction (both increase together, or both decrease together), the correlation is:
solution: When two variables move/change in the same direction — that is, when one increases the other also tends to increase, and when one decreases the other also tends to decrease (they rise and fall together) — the correlation between them is positive (a positive/direct correlation). For example, income and consumption usually have a positive correlation (as income rises, consumption tends to rise), and height and weight are positively correlated. So a positive correlation means the two variables move together in the same direction. Understanding positive correlation is a key prelims-relevant point. Positive correlation is when two variables move in the same direction (both increase together, or both decrease together).

stem: When two variables move in OPPOSITE directions (one increases as the other decreases), the correlation is:
solution: When two variables move/change in opposite directions — that is, when one increases the other tends to decrease, and vice versa (they move inversely) — the correlation between them is negative (a negative/inverse correlation). For example, the price of a good and the quantity demanded of it usually have a negative correlation (as the price rises, the quantity demanded tends to fall — the law of demand). So a negative correlation means the two variables move in opposite directions. Understanding negative correlation is a key prelims-relevant point. Negative correlation is when two variables move in opposite directions (one increases as the other decreases).

stem: When there is NO relationship between two variables (they do not move together in any consistent way), the correlation is said to be:
solution: When there is no relationship/association between two variables — that is, they do not move/change together in any consistent or systematic way (a change in one is not accompanied by any regular change in the other) — the correlation is said to be zero (no correlation). For example, there is likely to be zero correlation between a person's shoe size and their intelligence, or between the amount of rainfall and the price of a stock — the two are unrelated. So zero correlation means the two variables are independent/unrelated (as far as any linear relationship goes). Understanding zero (no) correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Zero (no) correlation means there is no consistent relationship between the two variables.

stem: The example of PRICE and quantity DEMANDED (as price rises, demand falls) is an example of __________ correlation.
solution: The relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded of it is an example of negative correlation: as the price rises, the quantity demanded tends to fall (and as the price falls, demand tends to rise) — the two move in opposite directions. This is the famous 'law of demand' in economics. So price and quantity demanded are negatively (inversely) correlated. (In contrast, price and quantity SUPPLIED are usually positively correlated — as price rises, supply tends to rise.) Understanding this economic example of negative correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Price and quantity demanded (price up, demand down) is an example of negative correlation.

stem: The example of INCOME and CONSUMPTION (as income rises, consumption tends to rise) is an example of __________ correlation.
solution: The relationship between income and consumption is an example of positive correlation: as a person's (or a country's) income rises, their consumption (spending on goods and services) tends to rise as well — the two move in the same direction. (This is consistent with the economic idea that consumption increases with income.) So income and consumption are positively (directly) correlated. Other examples of positive correlation include height and weight, and the amount of study and marks obtained. Understanding this economic example of positive correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Income and consumption (income up, consumption up) is an example of positive correlation.

stem: A graph in which the pairs of values of two variables are plotted as points (to see the pattern of their relationship) is called a:
solution: A scatter diagram (scatter plot) is a graph in which the pairs of values of two variables are plotted as points — with the values of one variable measured along the horizontal (x) axis and the values of the other along the vertical (y) axis, and each pair of values shown as a single point (dot). The overall pattern/scatter of the plotted points reveals the nature of the relationship between the two variables: if the points tend to rise from lower-left to upper-right, there is positive correlation; if they fall from upper-left to lower-right, negative correlation; if they cluster tightly along a line, strong correlation; and if they are scattered randomly with no pattern, little or no correlation. So the scatter diagram is a simple visual method of studying correlation. Understanding the scatter diagram is a key prelims-relevant point. A scatter diagram plots the pairs of values of two variables as points, to show the pattern of their relationship (correlation).

stem: In a scatter diagram, if the points tend to rise together from the lower-left to the upper-right, it indicates __________ correlation.
solution: In a scatter diagram, if the plotted points tend to rise together from the lower-left toward the upper-right (i.e., higher values of one variable go with higher values of the other), it indicates positive correlation — the two variables move in the same direction. (The more closely the points cluster along an upward-sloping line, the stronger the positive correlation.) By contrast, points falling from the upper-left to the lower-right indicate negative correlation, and points scattered randomly with no clear direction indicate little or no correlation. So an upward-rising pattern of points = positive correlation. Understanding this reading of a scatter diagram is a prelims-relevant point. In a scatter diagram, points rising from lower-left to upper-right indicate positive correlation.

stem: In a scatter diagram, if the points tend to fall from the upper-left to the lower-right, it indicates __________ correlation.
solution: In a scatter diagram, if the plotted points tend to fall from the upper-left toward the lower-right (i.e., higher values of one variable go with lower values of the other), it indicates negative correlation — the two variables move in opposite directions. (The more closely the points cluster along a downward-sloping line, the stronger the negative correlation.) So a downward-falling pattern of points = negative correlation. (An upward-rising pattern = positive correlation; a random scatter = no correlation.) Understanding this reading of a scatter diagram is a prelims-relevant point. In a scatter diagram, points falling from upper-left to lower-right indicate negative correlation.

stem: The measure that gives a single number expressing the degree (strength) and direction of the linear correlation between two variables is called the __________.
solution: The coefficient of correlation is the measure that gives a single number expressing both the degree (strength) and the direction of the (linear) correlation between two variables. The most common one is Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (denoted 'r'). Its sign (+ or −) shows the direction of the correlation (positive or negative), and its magnitude (how close it is to 1) shows the strength/degree of the correlation. So, instead of just a visual impression (from a scatter diagram), the coefficient of correlation gives a precise numerical measure of the relationship. Understanding the coefficient of correlation is a key prelims-relevant point. The coefficient of correlation is a single number expressing the degree (strength) and direction of the linear correlation between two variables.

stem: The coefficient of correlation (r) always lies between:
solution: The coefficient of correlation (r) always lies between −1 and +1 (inclusive) — that is, −1 ≤ r ≤ +1. Its value is never less than −1 or more than +1. The value indicates both the direction and the strength of the correlation: r = +1 means perfect positive correlation; r = −1 means perfect negative correlation; r = 0 means no (linear) correlation; and values in between indicate the degree (the closer to +1 or −1, the stronger the correlation; the closer to 0, the weaker). So r is always a number from −1 to +1. Understanding the range of r (−1 to +1) is a key prelims-relevant point. The coefficient of correlation (r) always lies between −1 and +1.

stem: A coefficient of correlation of r = +1 indicates:
options: perfect positive correlation (the two variables move together perfectly in the same direction)
solution: A coefficient of correlation of r = +1 indicates perfect positive correlation — meaning the two variables have a perfect, exact linear relationship in the same direction: as one increases, the other increases in perfect proportion (in a scatter diagram, all the points would lie exactly on an upward-sloping straight line). This is the strongest possible positive correlation. (Similarly, r = −1 indicates perfect negative correlation — a perfect inverse linear relationship. And r = 0 indicates no linear correlation.) So r = +1 means a perfect, direct linear relationship. Understanding what r = +1 means is a prelims-relevant point. A coefficient of correlation of r = +1 indicates perfect positive correlation.

stem: A coefficient of correlation of r = −1 indicates:
options: perfect negative correlation (perfect inverse linear relationship)
solution: A coefficient of correlation of r = −1 indicates perfect negative correlation — meaning the two variables have a perfect, exact linear relationship in opposite directions: as one increases, the other decreases in perfect proportion (in a scatter diagram, all the points would lie exactly on a downward-sloping straight line). This is the strongest possible negative (inverse) correlation. (Similarly, r = +1 is perfect positive correlation, and r = 0 is no linear correlation.) So r = −1 means a perfect, inverse linear relationship. Understanding what r = −1 means is a prelims-relevant point. A coefficient of correlation of r = −1 indicates perfect negative correlation.

stem: A coefficient of correlation of r = 0 indicates:
options: no (linear) correlation between the two variables
solution: A coefficient of correlation of r = 0 indicates no (linear) correlation between the two variables — i.e., there is no linear relationship/association between them (a change in one is not linearly associated with any change in the other; in a scatter diagram, the points would be scattered randomly with no upward or downward trend). So r = 0 means the two variables are (linearly) unrelated/independent. (Note: r = 0 rules out only a LINEAR relationship — the variables could still have some non-linear relationship that r does not capture.) Understanding what r = 0 means is a prelims-relevant point. A coefficient of correlation of r = 0 indicates no (linear) correlation between the two variables.

stem: The commonly used method that gives a precise mathematical measure of correlation (using all the values) is __________ coefficient of correlation.
solution: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation is the most commonly used method that gives a precise mathematical (numerical) measure of the degree of (linear) correlation between two variables — it uses all the values of both variables in its calculation (through a formula involving their deviations and standard deviations, or their products). It is denoted by 'r' and always lies between −1 and +1. (Another method, Spearman's rank correlation, measures the correlation between the ranks of the variables — useful for qualitative/ranked data.) So Karl Pearson's coefficient is the standard, precise measure of correlation. Understanding Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation is the commonly-used precise mathematical measure of correlation (using all the values).

stem: The method of correlation that measures the association between the RANKS of two variables (useful for qualitative characteristics that can be ranked) is __________ rank correlation.
solution: Spearman's rank correlation (the rank correlation coefficient) is the method that measures the degree of association/correlation between the ranks of two variables — that is, between the orderings/rankings of the items on the two variables. It is especially useful when the data are qualitative characteristics that can be ranked (but not exactly measured) — such as beauty, honesty, intelligence, or the rankings given by two judges — where Karl Pearson's method (which needs numerical measurements) cannot be applied. It is also used when the actual data are given as ranks. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient also lies between −1 and +1. Understanding Spearman's rank correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Spearman's rank correlation measures the association between the ranks of two variables (useful for rankable qualitative characteristics).

stem: A VERY IMPORTANT caution about correlation is that correlation does NOT necessarily imply __________ (that one variable causes the other).
solution: A very important caution about correlation is that 'correlation does not (necessarily) imply causation' — that is, the mere fact that two variables are correlated (move together) does NOT prove that one causes the other. Two variables may be correlated for reasons other than a direct cause-effect link: the relationship might be a coincidence (chance); or both variables might be influenced by some third, common factor (which causes them both to move together); or the causation might run the other way; and so on. For example, ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated (both rise in summer), but neither causes the other — both are driven by the hot weather (a third factor). So one must be careful not to jump from correlation to a conclusion about causation. Understanding this crucial caution is a key prelims-relevant point. Correlation does not necessarily imply causation — two correlated variables need not have a cause-effect relationship (there may be a third factor or coincidence).

stem: Two variables may show correlation without any direct cause-effect link because of the influence of a __________ factor affecting both.
solution: Two variables may show correlation (appear to move together) without any direct cause-effect link between them because of the influence of a third (common/hidden) factor that affects both of them. For example, the number of ice creams sold and the number of drowning incidents are positively correlated — but not because one causes the other; rather, both are influenced by a third factor, the hot summer weather (which increases both swimming/drowning and ice-cream sales). Such correlation, caused by a common third factor (and not by any direct link between the two variables), is sometimes called 'spurious' or 'nonsense' correlation. This is a key reason why correlation does not prove causation. Understanding the role of a third factor is a prelims-relevant point. Two variables may be correlated without a cause-effect link because a third (common) factor affects both of them.

stem: If the value of the correlation coefficient is close to +1 or −1 (say ±0.9), it indicates a __________ correlation.
solution: If the value of the correlation coefficient (r) is close to +1 or −1 (for example, r = +0.9 or r = −0.9), it indicates a strong (high degree of) correlation between the two variables — the two variables are closely/strongly related (in a scatter diagram, the points would cluster tightly along a line). The closer |r| is to 1, the stronger the correlation; the closer |r| is to 0, the weaker the correlation. (The sign, + or −, gives the direction; the magnitude gives the strength.) So r near ±1 = strong correlation, and r near 0 = weak/no correlation. Understanding how the magnitude of r indicates strength is a prelims-relevant point. A correlation coefficient close to +1 or −1 (like ±0.9) indicates a strong correlation.

stem: Assertion (A): A high correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other. Reason (R): The correlation could be due to chance, or to a third factor influencing both variables. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that a high correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other (correlation ≠ causation). And the reason is (R) that the observed correlation could arise from causes other than a direct cause-effect link — for example, it could be due to chance/coincidence, or it could be caused by a third (common) factor that influences both variables (making them move together without either causing the other). Because the correlation can have these non-causal explanations, a high correlation, by itself, cannot establish that one variable causes the other — so R correctly explains why correlation does not prove causation (A). Understanding this crucial caution (and its reasons) is a key prelims-relevant point. A high correlation does not prove causation because the correlation could be due to chance or to a third factor influencing both variables.

stem: Correlation in which the ratio of change between the two variables is constant (so that a scatter of points falls along a straight line) is called __________ correlation.
solution: Linear correlation is correlation in which the amount/ratio of change between the two variables is (approximately) constant — so that, when plotted, the points of the scatter diagram tend to fall along (cluster around) a straight line. In other words, the relationship between the two variables can be represented by a straight line (a constant rate of change). (Non-linear or curvilinear correlation, by contrast, is where the ratio of change is not constant, and the points fall along a curve rather than a straight line.) Karl Pearson's coefficient measures linear correlation. Understanding linear correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Linear correlation is where the ratio of change between the variables is constant, so the points fall along a straight line.

stem: The statistical measure of the joint variation of two variables (the average of the products of their deviations from their means) is called the:
solution: The covariance is the statistical measure of the joint variation of two variables — how they vary together. It is calculated as the average of the products of the deviations of the two variables from their respective means: Cov(x,y) = Σ[(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)] ÷ N. A positive covariance indicates that the two variables tend to move in the same direction (positive correlation), and a negative covariance that they move in opposite directions (negative correlation). The covariance is the basis of Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient (r = covariance ÷ (σx·σy), i.e., the covariance standardised by dividing by the product of the two standard deviations). Understanding covariance is a prelims-relevant point. Covariance is the average of the products of the deviations of two variables from their means — measuring their joint variation.

stem: A useful property of Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) is that it is a __________ number (has no units), so it can compare relationships measured in different units.
solution: A useful property of Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) is that it is a pure number — it is unit-free (dimensionless), having no units of measurement. This is because r is a ratio (the covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations), in which the units cancel out. Being unit-free is very useful: it means r can be used to compare the strength/direction of relationships between variables measured in completely different units (e.g., the correlation of height-and-weight can be compared with that of income-and-consumption), and its value (always between −1 and +1) has a consistent meaning regardless of the units. Understanding that r is a pure/unit-free number is a prelims-relevant point. Karl Pearson's r is a pure (unit-free/dimensionless) number, so it can compare relationships measured in different units.

stem: The correlation coefficient (r) is independent of the __________ — changing the origin or the scale (units) of the variables does not change its value.
solution: A property of the correlation coefficient (r) is that it is independent of the change of origin and change of scale of the variables — meaning that if you add/subtract a constant from the values (change of origin) or multiply/divide the values by a constant (change of scale/units) of either or both variables, the value of r does not change. For example, whether temperature is measured in Celsius or Fahrenheit, or income in rupees or thousands of rupees, the correlation coefficient between the variables stays the same. This property (invariance to change of origin and scale) makes r a stable, reliable measure of the relationship (and it is what makes r unit-free). Understanding this property is a prelims-relevant point. The correlation coefficient r is independent of the change of origin and scale — changing the origin or units does not change r.

stem: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is calculated using the formula involving Σd², where d is the __________ between the two ranks of each item.
solution: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is calculated using the formula r = 1 − [6Σd² ÷ N(N² − 1)], where 'd' is the difference between the two ranks of each item (the rank on the first variable minus the rank on the second variable), Σd² is the sum of the squares of these rank-differences, and N is the number of items. So, for each item, you find how differently it is ranked on the two variables (the rank difference d), square these differences, sum them (Σd²), and plug into the formula. This gives a correlation coefficient (between −1 and +1) based on the ranks. Understanding that d is the difference between the two ranks (in Spearman's formula) is a prelims-relevant point. In Spearman's rank correlation, d is the difference between the two ranks of each item (and the formula uses Σd²).

stem: Simple correlation involves __________ variables, whereas multiple correlation involves more than two.
solution: Simple correlation is the study of the correlation/relationship between two variables only (e.g., between income and consumption). Multiple correlation, by contrast, involves the study of the relationship among more than two variables together (e.g., how one variable relates to two or more others jointly — like how crop yield relates to both rainfall AND fertiliser). (There is also 'partial correlation' — studying the relationship between two variables while holding the effect of other variables constant.) So the distinction is by the number of variables: simple = two; multiple = more than two. Understanding simple vs multiple correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Simple correlation involves two variables, whereas multiple correlation involves more than two variables.

stem: A LIMITATION of the scatter diagram method is that it:
options: gives an exact numerical value of correlation
shows only the general nature/direction of the correlation (and roughly its strength), but does NOT give an exact numerical measure of it
solution: A limitation of the scatter diagram method (of studying correlation) is that it shows only the general nature and direction of the correlation — whether it is positive, negative, or absent, and a rough sense of whether it is strong or weak (from how tightly the points cluster) — but it does NOT give an exact numerical measure of the degree/strength of correlation. From a scatter diagram, you can see and roughly judge the relationship, but you cannot read off a precise number for how strong it is. (For an exact numerical measure, one must calculate a correlation coefficient, like Karl Pearson's r.) So the scatter diagram is a good first, visual step, but it is not precise. Understanding this limitation of the scatter diagram is a prelims-relevant point. A limitation of the scatter diagram is that it shows only the general nature/direction of correlation, not an exact numerical measure.

stem: An ADVANTAGE of the scatter diagram is that it is a __________ and easily-understood first step, and it is not affected by extreme values in the way a calculated coefficient can be.
solution: An advantage of the scatter diagram (as a method of studying correlation) is that it is a simple, visual, non-mathematical first step — easy to draw and easily understood (you can see the relationship at a glance, without any calculation), which makes it a good starting point for studying the correlation between two variables. Another advantage: the scatter diagram is not unduly affected by extreme values (outliers stand out as isolated points but do not distort the overall visual pattern the way they can distort a calculated statistic), and it can reveal the nature of the relationship (including non-linear patterns). So the scatter diagram is simple, quick, and visual. (Its limitation is that it does not give an exact numerical measure.) Understanding this advantage is a prelims-relevant point. The scatter diagram is a simple, visual first step that is easily understood and not distorted by extreme values.

stem: When ALL the points of a scatter diagram lie EXACTLY on a single straight line, the correlation is:
solution: When all the points of a scatter diagram lie exactly on a single straight line, the correlation between the two variables is perfect — meaning r = +1 (if the line slopes upward, a perfect positive correlation) or r = −1 (if the line slopes downward, a perfect negative correlation). This is because every point lying exactly on a line means there is an exact, perfect linear relationship between the two variables (no scatter/deviation at all). So all points on a straight line = perfect correlation (r = ±1). (The more scattered the points are away from a line, the weaker the correlation, toward r = 0.) Understanding that points exactly on a line mean perfect correlation is a prelims-relevant point. When all the scatter-diagram points lie exactly on a straight line, the correlation is perfect (r = +1 or −1).

stem: The relationship between PRICE and quantity SUPPLIED (as price rises, supply tends to rise) is an example of __________ correlation.
solution: The relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied of it is an example of positive correlation: as the price rises, the quantity supplied tends to rise (producers are willing to supply more at higher prices), and as the price falls, supply tends to fall — the two move in the same direction. (This is the 'law of supply' in economics.) So price and quantity supplied are positively (directly) correlated. (This contrasts with price and quantity DEMANDED, which are negatively correlated — the law of demand.) Understanding this economic example of positive correlation is a prelims-relevant point. Price and quantity supplied (price up, supply up) is an example of positive correlation.

stem: Spearman's rank correlation is especially useful when the data are given as, or can only be, __________.
options: ranks (or qualitative characteristics that can be ranked but not exactly measured)
solution: Spearman's rank correlation is especially useful when the data are given as ranks, or when the characteristics being studied are qualitative and can only be ranked (ordered) but not exactly measured numerically — such as beauty, intelligence, honesty, efficiency, or the preferences/rankings given by judges. In such cases, Karl Pearson's coefficient (which requires actual numerical measurements) cannot be applied, but the items CAN be ranked on each characteristic, and Spearman's rank correlation can then measure the association between the two sets of ranks. So Spearman's method handles ranked/rankable qualitative data. (It is also convenient when the numerical data are irregular or when only ranks are available.) Understanding when Spearman's rank correlation is used is a prelims-relevant point. Spearman's rank correlation is especially useful when the data are ranks, or qualitative characteristics that can be ranked but not exactly measured.

stem: The correlation coefficient measures only the __________ relationship between two variables (a value of r = 0 does not rule out a non-linear relationship).
solution: The (Karl Pearson) correlation coefficient (r) measures only the linear (straight-line) relationship between two variables — i.e., how well the relationship can be described by a straight line. A value of r = 0 means there is no LINEAR relationship, but it does NOT rule out the possibility of a non-linear (curved) relationship: the two variables could be strongly related in a curved/non-linear way, yet still have r = 0 (because r captures only the linear part). So r = 0 means 'no linear correlation', not necessarily 'no relationship at all'. This is an important limitation to keep in mind when interpreting the correlation coefficient. Understanding that r measures only linear correlation is a prelims-relevant point. The correlation coefficient measures only the linear relationship; r = 0 does not rule out a non-linear relationship.

stem: A correlation that appears to exist between two variables but is actually meaningless (due to coincidence or a third factor, with no real connection) is called a __________ correlation.
solution: A spurious correlation (also called a 'nonsense' correlation) is a correlation that appears to exist between two variables (they seem to move together statistically) but is actually meaningless — there is no real, direct connection or cause-effect relationship between them. The apparent correlation arises by pure coincidence/chance, or because both variables are influenced by some third (common) factor (so they move together without either causing or being related to the other). A classic example is the correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning deaths (both driven by hot weather, not by each other). Spurious correlations are exactly why 'correlation does not imply causation' and why correlations must be interpreted carefully. Understanding spurious/nonsense correlation is a prelims-relevant point. A spurious (nonsense) correlation appears to exist but is meaningless — due to coincidence or a third factor, with no real connection.

stem: The square of the correlation coefficient (r²), which indicates the proportion of the variation in one variable that is explained by the other, is called the coefficient of:
solution: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient (r²). It indicates the proportion (fraction/percentage) of the variation in one variable that is 'explained by' (associated with) its linear relationship with the other variable. For example, if r = 0.8, then r² = 0.64, meaning that about 64% of the variation in one variable can be explained by (is associated with) the other — and the remaining 36% is due to other factors. The coefficient of determination (r²) thus gives a sense of how much of the variation the correlation accounts for, and it is always between 0 and 1. Understanding the coefficient of determination (r²) is a prelims-relevant point. The coefficient of determination (r²) is the square of r, indicating the proportion of the variation in one variable explained by the other.

stem: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation is defined as the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their __________.
solution: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (r) is defined as the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations: r = Cov(x,y) ÷ (σx · σy), where Cov(x,y) is the covariance of x and y, and σx and σy are the standard deviations of x and y respectively. In effect, r 'standardises' the covariance (which measures the joint variation) by dividing it by the product of the two standard deviations (which measure the individual variations) — this is what makes r a pure, unit-free number lying between −1 and +1. Understanding this definition of Pearson's r (covariance ÷ product of SDs) is a prelims-relevant point. Karl Pearson's r = covariance of the two variables ÷ the product of their standard deviations.

stem: The FIRST/simplest step usually taken to study whether two variables are correlated is to:
options: draw a scatter diagram (to see the pattern visually)
solution: The first/simplest step usually taken to study whether (and how) two variables are correlated is to draw a scatter diagram — plotting the pairs of values as points to see the pattern visually. The scatter diagram gives an immediate, easy visual impression of whether there is a relationship, in which direction (positive/negative), and roughly how strong it is (how tightly the points cluster) — all without any calculation. So it is the natural starting point for correlation analysis (a quick visual check), after which, if a precise measure is needed, a correlation coefficient can be calculated. Understanding that the scatter diagram is the usual first step is a prelims-relevant point. The first/simplest step to study correlation is to draw a scatter diagram, to see the pattern visually.

stem: The degree of correlation can be described as perfect, high (strong), moderate, low (weak), or __________ (absent).
solution: The degree (strength) of correlation is often described in categories based on the value of the correlation coefficient (r): perfect correlation (r = ±1); high/strong correlation (|r| close to 1, e.g., 0.75 to 1); moderate correlation (|r| in the middle range, e.g., about 0.25 to 0.75); low/weak correlation (|r| small, e.g., 0 to 0.25); and zero/absent (no) correlation (r = 0). So the categories run from perfect, through high, moderate, and low, down to zero (no correlation) — describing how strongly the two variables are related. Understanding this scale of the degree of correlation is a prelims-relevant point. The degree of correlation can be perfect, high (strong), moderate, low (weak), or zero (absent).

stem: A study of the relationship between the amount of RAINFALL and CROP yield would typically show a __________ correlation (up to a point).
solution: A study of the relationship between the amount of rainfall and crop yield would typically show a positive correlation (at least up to a point) — because, generally, more rainfall (adequate water) leads to better crop growth and a higher yield (the two increase together). (Beyond a certain point, however, excessive rainfall/flooding can harm crops, so the relationship may become non-linear — turning negative at very high rainfall. But within the normal range, more rain tends to mean more yield — a positive correlation.) This is a common real-world example of positive correlation in economics/agriculture. Understanding this example is a prelims-relevant point. Rainfall and crop yield typically show a positive correlation (up to a point) — more rain generally means a higher yield.

stem: Correlation analysis is useful in economics because it helps to __________ between economic variables (like income and consumption, or price and demand).
solution: Correlation analysis is useful in economics because it helps to identify and measure the relationships (associations) between economic variables — such as between income and consumption, price and demand, price and supply, advertising and sales, rainfall and agricultural output, and so on. By revealing whether such variables are related, in which direction, and how strongly, correlation analysis helps economists to understand economic behaviour, test economic theories/hypotheses, and make predictions and policies (and it is the basis for further techniques like regression, which estimate and predict one variable from another). So correlation is a valuable tool for studying economic relationships. Understanding the usefulness of correlation in economics is a prelims-relevant point. Correlation analysis is useful in economics because it helps to identify and measure the relationships between economic variables.

stem: The correlation coefficient is a __________ measure — its value stays the same whether we call it 'the correlation of x with y' or 'the correlation of y with x'.
solution: The correlation coefficient is a symmetric measure — the correlation between x and y is the same as the correlation between y and x (i.e., r(x,y) = r(y,x)). It simply measures the strength and direction of the association between the two variables, without distinguishing which one is the 'cause' or the 'independent' variable and which is the 'effect' or 'dependent' variable — so the order does not matter, and the value is the same either way. (This symmetry is one reason correlation, by itself, does not indicate the direction of causation — it treats the two variables symmetrically.) Understanding that correlation is symmetric is a prelims-relevant point. The correlation coefficient is symmetric — its value is the same whether taken as the correlation of x with y or of y with x.

stem: If two variables are UNRELATED (independent), their correlation coefficient will be __________ (or close to it).
solution: If two variables are unrelated (independent) — i.e., there is no (linear) relationship between them, so a change in one is not associated with any consistent change in the other — their correlation coefficient will be 0 (zero), or close to zero. This reflects the absence of any linear correlation. (For example, a person's shoe size and their exam marks are likely unrelated, giving a correlation near 0.) So independence/no relationship corresponds to r ≈ 0. (Conversely, a strong relationship gives r close to +1 or −1.) Understanding that unrelated variables give r ≈ 0 is a prelims-relevant point. If two variables are unrelated (independent), their correlation coefficient is 0 (or close to it).

stem: A study of the number of hours studied and the marks obtained by students would typically show a __________ correlation.
solution: A study of the number of hours studied and the marks obtained by students would typically show a positive correlation — because, in general, students who study more hours tend to obtain higher marks (the two increase together, moving in the same direction). (Of course, the correlation is not perfect — other factors like ability, method of study, and health also matter — but the general tendency is positive.) This is a common everyday example of positive correlation. Understanding this example is a prelims-relevant point. The number of hours studied and the marks obtained typically show a positive correlation (more study, higher marks).

stem: In Spearman's rank correlation formula, r = 1 − [6Σd² ÷ N(N² − 1)], the 'N' stands for the:
solution: In Spearman's rank correlation formula, r = 1 − [6Σd² ÷ N(N² − 1)], the 'N' stands for the number of items (pairs of observations) being ranked — i.e., how many items/individuals are being ranked on each of the two variables. (Σd² is the sum of the squares of the rank-differences, and the '6' is a constant in the formula.) So N is the count of the ranked items. For example, if 10 students are ranked on two subjects, N = 10. Understanding what N stands for in Spearman's formula is a prelims-relevant point. In Spearman's rank correlation formula, N stands for the number of items (pairs) being ranked.

stem: Both Karl Pearson's coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient always lie within the range:
solution: Both Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient always lie within the range −1 to +1 (inclusive). In both cases, the value indicates the direction (sign: + for positive, − for negative) and the strength (magnitude: closer to 1 = stronger, closer to 0 = weaker) of the correlation, with +1 = perfect positive, −1 = perfect negative, and 0 = no correlation. So, whether you use Pearson's (for measured data) or Spearman's (for ranked data), the coefficient always falls between −1 and +1. Understanding that both coefficients range from −1 to +1 is a prelims-relevant point. Both Karl Pearson's and Spearman's correlation coefficients always lie between −1 and +1.

stem: A classic example illustrating that 'correlation is not causation' is the correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning deaths, which is really caused by:
options: a third factor — hot summer weather (which increases both)
solution: A classic example illustrating that 'correlation is not causation' is the positive correlation between ice-cream sales and the number of drowning deaths — these two rise and fall together (they are correlated). But neither causes the other (eating ice cream does not cause drowning, nor vice versa). The real explanation is a third (common) factor: hot summer weather — in hot weather, more people buy ice cream AND more people go swimming (so more drownings occur). So the hot weather drives both, creating a spurious correlation between them. This example vividly shows why a correlation does not prove a cause-effect link (there may be a hidden common cause). Understanding this classic example is a prelims-relevant point. The ice-cream-sales/drowning correlation is really caused by a third factor — hot summer weather (which increases both) — illustrating that correlation is not causation.

stem: Correlation differs from regression in that correlation measures the __________ of the relationship, whereas regression is used to ESTIMATE/predict one variable from another.
solution: Correlation and regression are related but different techniques for studying the relationship between two variables. Correlation measures the degree/strength and direction of the relationship (association) between two variables — it tells us how closely and in which direction they are related (giving a single number, r, between −1 and +1). Regression, on the other hand, goes a step further: it establishes a mathematical relationship (an equation/line) between the variables that can be used to estimate or predict the value of one variable (the dependent variable) from a given value of the other (the independent variable). So, correlation = how strongly related; regression = predicting one from the other. Understanding this difference is a prelims-relevant point. Correlation measures the strength and direction of the relationship, whereas regression is used to estimate/predict one variable from another.

stem: A HIGH degree of correlation between two variables means that:
options: they are closely/strongly related (change together very consistently)
solution: A high degree of correlation between two variables (a correlation coefficient close to +1 or −1) means that the two variables are closely/strongly related — they change together very consistently (in a scatter diagram, the points cluster tightly along a line). A high positive correlation means they strongly move together in the same direction; a high negative correlation, strongly in opposite directions. Importantly, though, a high correlation does NOT by itself mean that one variable causes the other (correlation is not causation) — it only means they are strongly associated/related. So high correlation = strong association (but not proof of causation). Understanding what a high degree of correlation means (and does not mean) is a prelims-relevant point. A high degree of correlation means the two variables are closely/strongly related (but it does not prove that one causes the other).

stem: Which of the following pairs would likely show a NEGATIVE correlation?
options: The price of a good and the quantity of it demanded
solution: Of the options, 'the price of a good and the quantity of it demanded' would likely show a negative correlation — because, by the law of demand, as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded of it tends to fall (they move in opposite directions). The other pairs would show positive correlations: income and consumption (both rise together), height and weight (taller people tend to weigh more), and study hours and marks (more study tends to mean higher marks) — all moving in the same direction. So the price-and-quantity-demanded pair is the negative one. Understanding which relationships are negative vs positive is a prelims-relevant point. Price and quantity demanded would likely show a negative correlation (price up, demand down), unlike the other pairs, which are positive.

stem: Assertion (A): A scatter diagram is a good starting point for studying correlation, but a correlation coefficient is needed for a precise measure. Reason (R): The scatter diagram shows the direction and rough strength of the relationship visually, while the coefficient gives an exact numerical value of the degree of correlation. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that a scatter diagram is a good starting point for studying correlation, but a correlation coefficient is needed for a precise measure. And the reason is (R) that the scatter diagram only shows the direction (positive/negative) and a rough sense of the strength of the relationship visually (from the pattern and tightness of the points) — it does NOT give an exact number; whereas the correlation coefficient (like Karl Pearson's r) gives an exact numerical value of the degree/strength of the correlation. So, because the scatter diagram gives only a visual, approximate picture while the coefficient gives the precise figure, one uses the scatter diagram first (for a quick visual sense) and then the coefficient for a precise measure — R correctly explains A. Understanding this (scatter diagram = visual first step; coefficient = precise measure) is a prelims-relevant point. A scatter diagram is a good visual starting point, but a correlation coefficient is needed because the diagram shows only the rough picture, while the coefficient gives the exact degree of correlation.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Correlation' is that:
options: Correlation measures the relationship (degree and direction) between two variables — which may be positive (moving together), negative (moving oppositely), or zero (unrelated) — studied through scatter diagrams and measured by the correlation coefficient (r, between −1 and +1); but a crucial caution is that correlation does NOT necessarily imply causation
Only one variable can be studied at a time
solution: The chapter conveys that correlation is a statistical tool for measuring and studying the relationship/association between two variables — the extent to which, and the direction in which, they change/move together. It explains the types/directions of correlation: positive correlation — when the two variables move in the same direction (both rise or both fall together, like income and consumption); negative correlation — when they move in opposite directions (one rises as the other falls, like price and quantity demanded); and zero (no) correlation — when there is no consistent relationship between them. It describes methods of studying correlation: the scatter diagram (a graph plotting the pairs of values as points, whose pattern — rising, falling, or random — shows the direction and rough strength of the correlation visually); and the coefficient of correlation — a single number that precisely measures the degree (strength) and direction of the (linear) correlation, most commonly Karl Pearson's coefficient (r), which always lies between −1 and +1 (r = +1 perfect positive, r = −1 perfect negative, r = 0 no linear correlation, and values in between showing intermediate strength), and, for ranked/qualitative data, Spearman's rank correlation. Above all, the chapter stresses the crucial caution that correlation does NOT necessarily imply causation — the fact that two variables are correlated does not prove that one causes the other, because the correlation could be due to chance/coincidence or to a third (common) factor affecting both (a 'spurious' correlation) — so one must be careful in interpreting correlations. Understanding what correlation is, its types, how it is studied (scatter diagrams) and measured (the correlation coefficient, −1 to +1), and the caution that correlation is not causation, is the central concern of this chapter. Correlation measures the degree and direction of the relationship between two variables (positive, negative, or zero), studied via scatter diagrams and measured by the coefficient r (−1 to +1) — but correlation does not necessarily imply causation.
